summary: Extends TWAMP, the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, to let the control and test protocols use different security modes at the same time. It also creates an IANA registry for further TWAMP features.

eli5.summary: Measuring network speed involves two conversations. This lets one conversation be locked while the other stays open, since they may need different protection.

questions: twamp control and test different modes
what is twamp mixed security mode
what is the twamp modes registry
subtitle: A TWAMP extension that lets the control channel be strongly protected while the test packets stay unauthenticated.

tldr.problem: In TWAMP, the test protocol inherited the security mode of the control protocol, so a stronger mode on control forced the same costly mode on the time-sensitive test packets.
tldr.mechanism: A new Modes value, 8 (bit position 3), lets the Control-Client choose Encrypted control with an Unauthenticated test protocol. The RFC also creates an IANA registry called the TWAMP Modes registry.
tldr.outcome: Control can get stronger integrity protection while the test protocol stays simple and efficient. The RFC updates RFC 5357 and has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 5618 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5357. The metadata for this document lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) is an extension of the One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP, RFC 4656). It has a control protocol, TWAMP-Control, which sets up measurement sessions, and a test protocol, TWAMP-Test, which sends the measurement packets.

This memo adds the option of using different security modes in the two protocols at once, called mixed security mode. The motivation is to let the low-packet-rate control protocol use a stronger mode of integrity protection than the test protocol. It keeps backward compatibility with existing TWAMP implementations. It also creates a new IANA registry for further TWAMP features.

When the Server and Control-Client agree on mixed mode during control connection setup, the Control-Client, Server, Session-Sender and Session-Reflector MUST all follow its requirements.
sections.eli5: TWAMP has two talks: a planning talk and a measuring talk. This memo lets the planning talk be well protected without slowing down the measuring talk.

sections.title: Choosing the Mode in Control Setup
sections.content:
Control connection setup works as in RFC 4656. The extension assigns one new bit position, 3, with value 8, meaning an Unauthenticated Test protocol with Encrypted Control. The full set of Modes values is 0 (Reserved), 1 (Unauthenticated), 2 (Authenticated), 4 (Encrypted) and 8 (the new mixed mode).

Before this, setting bit position 0, 1 or 2 chose the Control mode and the Test protocol inherited it. When the Control-Client sets bit position 3, it SHALL stop that inheritance. If the Test mode should match the Control mode, the client sets the matching bit (0, 1 or 2) as well. Control security is identical in Authenticated and Encrypted modes, so a single new bit is enough.

The Server's Server-Greeting carries a Modes field that is the bit-wise OR of the modes it is willing to support. The last four bits of the 32-bit field are used, and when no other features are active the first 28 bits MUST be zero. A conforming client MAY ignore those first 28 bits or MAY support other features signalled there.
sections.eli5: It is like picking a lock setting for each door separately. A new switch says: lock the planning door tightly, but leave the measuring door unlocked.

sections.title: Test Sender and Reflector Behaviour
sections.content:
The TWAMP-Test protocol is like OWAMP-Test, except that the Session-Reflector sends a test packet back for each one it receives. With this extension, Unauthenticated mode can be used in TWAMP-Test regardless of the mode used in TWAMP-Control.

The extensions become REQUIRED once three things have happened: the Server has indicated support for mixed mode, the Control-Client has selected it in its Set-Up-Response, and the Server has answered with a zero Accept field in the Server-Start message.

Both the Session-Sender and the Session-Reflector MUST support the mixed security mode. The Sender follows the packet format procedures in RFC 4656 and RFC 5357, and the send schedule is not used in TWAMP. The Reflector follows the procedures in RFC 5357.
sections.eli5: Once both sides agree on the new setting, the one who sends measuring pings and the one who bounces them back must both know how to use it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mixed mode permits stronger protection on TWAMP-Control while putting the emphasis on accuracy or efficiency in TWAMP-Test. The RFC argues this can raise overall security compared with the older options, where resource constraints might have forced weaker security on the control protocol. This holds when use of unauthenticated TWAMP-Test is not a significant concern.

The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks still apply, as described in RFC 4656 and RFC 5357.
sections.eli5: Because the planning talk is locked tight, people cannot easily mess up the setup, and the quick measuring talk can stay fast.

sections.title: The TWAMP Modes Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a TWAMP Modes registry for the Modes field. Modes are currently single bits in the 32-bit field, though more complex encodings may be used later, so the registry can hold a total of 2^32 possible assignments.

Because the registry is large and TWAMP is an IETF protocol, it must be updated only by "IETF Review" as specified in RFC 5226. New features are expected to take monotonically increasing single bit positions in the range 0 to 31, unless there is a good reason to do otherwise. No experimental values are currently assigned. The initial contents are the five values 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 listed above.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps a public list of every switch setting and what it means, so nobody picks the same switch for two different jobs.
